text:
**Richard Stallman** (b. March 16, 1953, New York City) is a prominent programmer and free software activist. Early on, he showed interest in computers and programming languages, working at IBM in high school and later at MIT's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, where he was a key figure in the hacker community. Stallman earned a physics degree from Harvard (1974) and briefly pursued graduate studies at MIT, focusing on programming and AI research.
In the early 1980s, reacting to the rise of proprietary software and restrictive licenses, Stallman launched the GNU Project in 1983 to create a free, Unix-compatible operating system. He founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1985 to support this movement and popularized the concept of “copyleft” through the GNU General Public License (GPL). Stallman developed critical GNU tools such as Emacs, GCC, and GDB, although the kernel (GNU Hurd) remained incomplete; Linux, developed by Linus Torvalds in 1991, combined with GNU tools to form GNU/Linux, a naming Stallman staunchly advocates for. Known for his unwavering philosophy emphasizing users’ freedom, Stallman has also faced controversies—most notably his 2019 resignation from MIT and FSF amid backlash over comments related to the Jeffrey Epstein scandal, though he later returned to the FSF board in 2021. Throughout his career, Stallman has been an ardent campaigner against software patents, DRM, and surveillance, promoting software freedom as a moral imperative.
